newsitem.title: USA: Too much antimony for Chinese threat to hurt-trade.
newsitem.headline: Too much antimony for Chinese threat to hurt-trade.

text.p: China's laying down of the antimony gauntlet in a bid to scare prices into recovery has left U.S. consumers and traders yawning on the sidelines as they prod domestic demand for signs of life.
"They make these announcements after they have shipped oodles and oodles of material, so you never see the effect," a U.S. producer source said. "It all has to be taken with a grain of salt."
Antimony prices have plunged to their lowest levels since 1993 to 1994. Metal prices are down over $1,000 since last summer to about $2,500 per tonne, with oxide at $2,650.
The slide finally provoked Chinese Antimony Producers Association to announce a 20 percent cut in production.
A U.S. trader who spoke to those attending the meeting said the Association was focusing on "reigning in" the smaller producers who were selling as much metal as they could to generate revenue.
China is the world's dominant supplier, accounting for about 50 to 55 million pounds of the 60 to 65 million pounds consumed by the United States each year, industry sources said.
"China is talking its book - prices are lousy. It's a gigantic poker game," a U.S. consumer said.
U.S. industry sources said if China's intention was real, it would take 90 to 120 days to have any effect. "There is a lot of material in Hong Kong and on the water," a source said.
Traders cautioned that China has threatened to cut minor metals production before to prop up prices, most notably in tungsten and bismuth, all without much success.
Chinese producers were saying that antimony prices of $3,500 a tonne were below their production costs, and had even attempted last summer to set a price floor of $4,800 a tonne.

Part of the problem faced by the Chinese is that the remnimbi is now fully convertible, making black market sales at inflated prices difficult, a trader said. "But the mines are also being starved of cash flow, which will probably mean there will be a price spike in six months to a year," he added.

Demand from the plastics sector for flame retardants - the biggest consumer - which uses oxide is said to be particularly weak. "I think the problem is less on the supply side than on the demand side," traders said.
Some industry sources said that since the last price spike, antimony may have lost market share to cheaper substitutes in fire retardants which is why demand is so weak.
